title: Client-Side and Browser Security Testing
learning_outcomes: Explain the main security concern and trust boundary involved in Client-Side and Browser Security Testing.
Choose an appropriate defensive control for Client-Side and Browser Security Testing and state the assumptions under which it works.
Define a safe, reproducible verification step for Client-Side and Browser Security Testing, including a relevant negative or failure case.

content.intro: This lesson belongs to Module 20: Web Application Security Testing Methodology. It builds practical understanding of Client-Side and Browser Security Testing with the syllabus subtopics retained below.
content.why_it_matters: Client-Side and Browser Security Testing turns a security intention into evidence, an operational owner, and a repeatable control. Keep untrusted values as data, use safe DOM or framework rendering and context-appropriate encoding, and add a regression test for the affected rendering path.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Client-Side and Browser Security Testing can be understood through this sequence: Define authorized scope → Form a test hypothesis → Record sanitized evidence → Retest the fix. Start with the application asset and trust boundary, state what secure behavior should occur, and identify the evidence that would prove or disprove it.

content_blocks.title: Connect the syllabus subtopics
content_blocks.text: The source curriculum groups this lesson around: 151.1 Evaluating XSS prevention; 151.2 Reviewing CSP and security headers; 151.3 Testing CORS and cross-origin assumptions; 151.4 Checking CSRF controls; 151.5 Inspecting client-side storage; 151.6 Reviewing iframe and messaging boundaries. Treat these points as a checklist, not a list to memorize: explain the risk, identify the root cause, select a control, and define a test for that control.

items.title: Scope
items.text: Identify the asset, principal, input, state, or boundary affected. State whether the example is local, owned, or explicitly authorized.

items.title: Control
items.text: Keep untrusted values as data, use safe DOM or framework rendering and context-appropriate encoding, and add a regression test for the affected rendering path.

items.title: Failure behavior
items.text: Include an invalid, denied, expired, malformed, repeated, or otherwise relevant boundary case. Fail safely without exposing secrets.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Record expected versus actual behavior, a sanitized request or test result, the root cause, the chosen fix, and the regression test.

content_blocks.expected_output: The response declares JSON content and asks caches not to retain this personalized response.
content_blocks.run_instructions: This is a schematic transcript for a local test app. Confirm actual headers in the browser network panel or an authorized HTTP client.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Use a clean local test account and synthetic data. Reset the test fixture after recording the result; do not include credentials or private data in the course report.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake and recovery
content_blocks.text: Do not confuse an observation with proof or rely on a UI-only restriction. Keep untrusted values as data, use safe DOM or framework rendering and context-appropriate encoding, and add a regression test for the affected rendering path. If evidence is ambiguous, reduce the test to one condition, inspect the application code/configuration, and repeat only within the permitted scope.

content_blocks.title: Execution and safety boundary
content_blocks.text: The current CodeLeaf playground is an HTML/CSS/JavaScript preview, not a secure runner for arbitrary server code. This example is a static reference unless the run instructions explicitly identify a supported local environment. Use a private local lab or a test system with written authorization; do not test unrelated public systems.

content.task: For “Client-Side and Browser Security Testing”, write a short security note or test in a local/owned application. Identify the expected secure behavior, at least one relevant failure case, and the evidence needed to prove the control works.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain the core rule for Client-Side and Browser Security Testing in your own words.
Name the trust boundary and the server-side control or policy that applies.
Specify a repeatable test for expected behavior and a relevant denied/failure path.
Use synthetic data and redact credentials, tokens, and personal information from evidence.
hints: Start by stating the asset, input, actor, or trust boundary and the expected secure behavior.
Change one condition at a time; record expected and actual outcomes with synthetic data.
Check the linked official reference for framework-specific settings and version-dependent behavior.
content.expected_output: A concise control explanation and a sanitized test record showing expected/actual behavior, one failure case, and a regression check.
recap: Client-Side and Browser Security Testing is a security boundary/control topic, not a standalone checklist item.
Keep untrusted values as data, use safe DOM or framework rendering and context-appropriate encoding, and add a regression test for the affected rendering path.
Retest fixes and record sanitized evidence; use only authorized environments.
